title: ABO & Rh Blood Grouping — Principle

references.label: AABB Technical Manual
references.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB)

summary: ABO and Rh(D) typing identify which red cell surface antigens a person carries, the single most critical piece of information for safe transfusion.
explanation: The ABO system is defined by A and B antigens on the red cell surface, with plasma naturally containing antibodies against whichever ABO antigen(s) an individual lacks (e.g. type A blood carries anti-B antibody) — this reciprocal relationship is what allows 'reverse grouping' to cross-check 'forward grouping' (see the related protocol). The Rh system's most clinically significant antigen is D: individuals with the D antigen are Rh-positive, those without it are Rh-negative. Transfusing ABO-incompatible red cells can trigger a rapid, potentially fatal intravascular hemolytic reaction because naturally occurring anti-A/anti-B antibodies are already present; Rh incompatibility does not cause an immediate reaction on first exposure but can cause sensitization, which matters especially in Rh-negative individuals who may be exposed to Rh-positive blood (e.g. in pregnancy or transfusion) and subsequently develop anti-D antibody.

comparison.left: Naturally occurring, present without prior exposure
comparison.right: Rh(D) antibodies: not naturally occurring — require prior sensitizing exposure

comparison.left: ABO-incompatible transfusion: immediate, severe hemolytic reaction risk
comparison.right: Rh-incompatible exposure: primarily a sensitization risk, especially relevant in pregnancy
